meta.title: Neuroscape Judge Program Study Guide & Quiz Bank
meta.source_rules: Neuroscape Comprehensive Rules v1.1, effective September 10, 2026 (Original game design: Alex Meader and Connor Hair. Rules development: Harrison Main, Scarlett Roberts, Alex Meader, Connor Hair)
meta.supersedes: Judge Program Study Guide v3.0 (Comprehensive Rules v1.0) and Edge Case Scenario Quiz Bank v2.0 (Rulebook v10.2)
meta.disclaimer: Community-created study material. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the creators of Neuroscape TCG.
meta.structure_note: Tiers are modeled on the Magic: The Gathering judge program (Judge Foundry / International Judge Program). There is no official Neuroscape judge program at time of writing.
meta.citation_format: All citations are Comprehensive Rules v1.0 rule numbers, e.g. 702.17a.

legend.changed: Flags a ruling that differs from an earlier rules version, either Rulebook v10.2 or Comprehensive Rules v1.0. Expect players to argue the old answer.
legend.confirmed: Ruling previously confirmed by community consensus or a designer on the Neuroscape Discord.
legend.cards: Real Genesis-set cards the scenario is built around.

tiers.name: Store Judge
tiers.tagline: Runs local events and answers the everyday questions.
tiers.scope: An N1 knows the turn structure cold, understands priority and swift checks, can resolve the cache without hesitation, and knows deck construction. They serve as the sole judge for casual, fun-first events at a local game store.
syllabus: Turn structure: the five phases and every step inside them
Priority and swift checks: who acts, when, and in what order
The cache: last in, first out, and when triggers resolve
RAM: running, refreshing, committing, and the Force Quit exception
Combat basics: declaring, blocking, and assigning damage
Deck construction and the four-copy limit
Starting the game, mulligans, and win/loss conditions
Force Quit: what qualifies, and where destroyed persistents go

exam.note: Closed book, untimed. Modeled on the MTG Level 1 exam: the goal is 'can you run a real event without it catching fire,' not rules recitation.

tiers.name: Competitive Judge
tiers.tagline: Floor judges competitive events and handles the hard interactions.
tiers.scope: An N2 handles the interactions that actually generate calls: layered continuous effects at a working level, state-based actions, replacement and prevention effects, keyword edge cases, and complex cache sequencing. They know which section of the Comprehensive Rules to open when unsure.
syllabus: Triggered abilities and why they usually cannot be responded to
Targeting: what targets, what merely affects, and illegal targets
The full state-based action list, especially bin versus destroy
Keywords in depth: Psychosis, Overrun, Trojan, Stamina, Duel
Replacement and prevention effects and their ordering
Iconic objects and the replacement effect that governs them
Costs, X, and additional costs
Damage marking versus defense reduction
Protocols, trojans, gear, and tethers as attachments

exam.note: Open book (Comprehensive Rules only), 90 minutes. Modeled on the MTG Level 2 exam, which is open-book and timed with a higher pass bar.

tiers.name: Head Judge
tiers.tagline: Head judges events, handles appeals, and certifies other judges.
tiers.scope: An N3 resolves appeals, performs backups, and rules on the interactions nobody else will touch: full layer stacks, looking back at objects and events, linked abilities, illegal action recovery, shortcuts, and every multiplayer and limited format.
syllabus: Layers 1 through 7 including all sublayers and timestamp rules
Looking back at objects and events, including synergy at the moment of a wipe
Linked abilities and what survives a zone change
Copying objects and what a copy knows
Handling illegal actions and correct game state restoration
Shortcuts: what they may and may not skip, and dispute resolution
Unstable resolution in full
2v2, free-for-all, draft, and sealed
Control versus ownership, especially where RAM is concerned

exam.note: Open book (Comprehensive Rules only), 80 minutes, proctored. Modeled on the MTG Level 3 exam. In MTG this level also requires an interview; that is a natural future addition here.

questions.title: Order of the Initialize Phase
questions.situation: Player A begins their turn. One of their characters lost its committed RAM last turn when a RAM card was destroyed. Player A wants to refresh first so that more RAM is available to auto-commit, and only then perform the system check.
questions.question: Can Player A reorder the steps of the Initialize Phase?

options.text: Yes. The active player chooses the order of steps within a phase.
No, but they may skip the System Check step entirely if they choose.
No. The steps are fixed: System Check, Refresh, Draw/Install, Force Quit.
Yes, but only if no opponent objects before priority is passed.

questions.explanation: The Initialize Phase runs four steps in strict order: System Check, Refresh, Draw/Install, Force Quit. Because System Check happens before Refresh, it evaluates RAM in the state it was left in at the end of the previous turn. Player A cannot refresh first to make more RAM available. If the character still lacks its required RAM at System Check, Player A's mainframe becomes unstable.
questions.changed: Under Rulebook v10.2 this was called a 'stability check.' The term no longer exists; the mechanic is now the Unstable keyword triggered from the System Check step.

questions.title: When does Netcheck happen?
questions.situation: Player A controls two persistents with 'on netcheck' abilities. They want to know exactly when those abilities fire relative to the rest of their turn.
questions.question: Where in the turn does the Netcheck Phase occur?

options.text: It is its own phase, occurring after Deploy and before Combat.
At the start of the Deploy Phase, before the active player takes any action.
During the Initialize Phase, immediately after the Refresh step.
At the end of the turn, during the Reset Phase.

questions.explanation: Netcheck is a full phase in its own right, sitting between Deploy and Combat. The turn runs Initialize, Deploy, Netcheck, Combat, Reset. No player naturally gains priority during Netcheck, and no swift check is created there as a turn-based action, though an effect can still create one.
questions.changed: Rulebook v10.2 placed netcheck at the start of the Deploy Phase. It is now a separate phase after Deploy. Any deck or ruling that relied on netcheck RAM being available for deploy-phase plays is now wrong.

questions.title: Ending the Deploy Phase
questions.situation: Player A has finished playing cards. The cache is empty. Player A passes priority. Player B has a swift script in hand and wants to hold it for the Deploy Phase.
questions.question: What happens when the active player passes priority with an empty cache during their Deploy Phase?

options.text: Priority passes to Player B, who may act before the phase ends.
A swift check is created automatically before the phase can end.
The phase ends only after every player has passed in succession.
The Deploy Phase ends immediately; Player B does not receive priority first.

questions.explanation: The Deploy Phase ends the moment the active player passes priority with an empty cache. The next player in turn order does not receive priority before the phase ends. Player B's window to act is a swift check. Created when someone plays a card or activates an ability, or at the start of the three combat steps that call for one.

questions.title: The Reset Phase in order
questions.situation: Player A's turn is ending. Several characters have damage marked on them, an 'until turn end' buff is active, and a persistent has an 'on turn end' triggered ability.
questions.question: In what order do the Reset Phase events occur?

options.text: Damage is cleared, then 'until turn end' effects expire, then 'on turn end' triggers resolve.
'On turn end' triggers resolve, then damage is cleared, then 'until turn end' effects expire.
All three happen simultaneously as a single state-based action.
'Until turn end' effects expire, then 'on turn end' triggers resolve, then damage is cleared.

questions.explanation: The Reset Phase places 'on turn end' triggers on the cache first. Once those have all resolved and the cache is empty, marked damage is removed from characters. Only then do 'until turn end' and 'this turn' effects expire. This ordering matters: an 'on turn end' trigger still sees the buff and still sees the damage.

questions.title: Who acts first in a swift check?
questions.situation: It is Player A's turn. The Declare Attackers step begins and a swift check is created as a turn-based action.
questions.question: Which player receives priority first?

options.text: The next non-active player in turn order.
The active player, because it is their turn.
Whichever player has the most refreshed RAM.
Neither. No player receives priority during combat steps.

questions.explanation: When a swift check is created. Whether by a player playing a card, activating an ability, or by a turn-based action. The next non-active player in turn order receives priority first. Priority then passes in turn order, and each player may act or pass.

questions.title: Playing a non-swift card
questions.situation: Player A is in their Deploy Phase. They play a script, and while that script is still on the cache, they want to play a character.
questions.question: May Player A play the character?

options.text: Yes. The active player may play any number of cards during Deploy.
Yes, but only if the character is also swift.
No. Only one card may be played per Deploy Phase.
No. A non-swift card may only be played during Deploy while the cache is empty.

questions.explanation: A non-swift card may be played only during its controller's Deploy Phase and only when the cache is empty. A swift card may be played any time its controller has priority. Once the script resolves and the cache empties, the active player automatically regains priority and may then play the character.

questions.title: Resolution order
questions.situation: Player A plays Script A. Player B responds with Script B. Player A responds with Script C. All players then pass in succession.
questions.question: In what order do the three scripts resolve?

options.text: A, then B, then C.
C, then B, then A.
The active player chooses the order.
All three resolve simultaneously.

questions.explanation: The cache resolves from the top down. The most recently added action resolves first. The rulebook phrases this as 'first in, last out.' State-based actions are checked after each action finishes resolving, and any triggers generated are placed on top of the cache and resolve before the next action.

questions.title: An ability whose source is destroyed
questions.situation: Player A activates Neosec Firestorm's ability, which deals 1 damage to up to three target characters. Player B responds with Delete, destroying Neosec Firestorm.
questions.question: Does the ability still deal damage?

options.text: No. Destroying the source removes its ability from the cache.
Yes, but it deals only half damage, rounded down.
Yes. Delete resolves first, then the ability resolves normally using last known information.
No. The ability is countered by the rules for having no source.

questions.explanation: An ability on the cache is an independent object with only the text of the ability that created it. It does not depend on its source continuing to exist. If the source is gone, the game uses that source's last known information. Delete resolves first, then the ability resolves and deals its damage.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by Soviet Panda and Kraotacen on Discord (April 2026).

questions.title: Force Quit versus destruction
questions.situation: Player A's 4-cost character is destroyed during combat. Later, during their own Initialize Phase, Player A force quits a different 3-cost character.
questions.question: How does the committed RAM return in each case?

options.text: Both return refreshed.
Both return running.
The destroyed character's RAM returns refreshed; the force quit character's RAM returns running.
The destroyed character's RAM returns running; the force quit character's RAM returns refreshed.

questions.explanation: When a character leaves play normally, its committed RAM becomes uncommitted and returns to the RAM bank running. Already spent for the turn. Force Quit is the exception: RAM from a force quit persistent returns refreshed and is immediately usable. This is a significant tempo distinction and a common source of judge calls.

questions.title: Auto-committing RAM
questions.situation: A cost-increasing effect enters play and raises Player A's 3-cost character to an effective cost of 4. Player A has one refreshed RAM and two running RAM in their bank.
questions.question: Which RAM becomes committed?

options.text: The controller chooses freely from any RAM in the bank.
The refreshed RAM, because refreshed RAM must be used before running RAM.
A running RAM, so the refreshed RAM stays available to pay costs.
None. The character is destroyed instead.

questions.explanation: When a character in play has fewer committed RAM cards than its RAM cost, RAM is automatically attached from its controller's bank as a state-based action, and refreshed RAM must be used before running RAM. The controller does not get to preserve their refreshed RAM.

questions.title: Excess committed RAM
questions.situation: A cost-increasing protocol leaves play. Player A's character now has 4 committed RAM but requires only 3.
questions.question: What happens to the excess RAM?

options.text: It stays committed; excess RAM is harmless.
The controller chooses one and it returns to the RAM bank refreshed.
The controller chooses one and it returns to the RAM bank running.
It is destroyed and put into the recycle bin.

questions.explanation: As a state-based action, the controller chooses which excess RAM becomes uncommitted, and it returns to the owner's RAM bank running. Note the contrast with Force Quit, where RAM comes back refreshed.

questions.title: Reboot is not refresh
questions.situation: Player A controls Admin, which is running. They play Hackathon, which reboots the abilities of all Hacker characters they control. Player A now wants to activate Admin's ability.
questions.question: Can they?

options.text: No. Rebooting restores ability use but does not refresh the character.
Yes. Rebooting returns the character to a refreshed state.
Yes, but only if the ability has no run symbol in its cost.
No. Abilities can never be activated during a swift check.

questions.explanation: Reboot and refresh are distinct. Rebooting removes a persistent's 'spent' state so it may activate an ability again; it does not turn the card upright. Whether Admin can now activate depends on whether the ability's cost requires running it. A running card cannot be run again to pay a cost.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by The Mystic Tobias on Discord: reboot restores abilities, characters do not get refreshed.

questions.title: Declaring attackers runs them
questions.situation: Player A declares attackers. Player B activates ACPD Drones' Detain ability, which runs target character, targeting one of the declared attackers.
questions.question: Does Detain remove the attacker from combat?

options.text: Yes. Running an attacker always removes it from combat.
No, but the attacker deals no combat damage this turn.
No. The attacker was already run as part of declaring the attack, so Detain does nothing.
Yes, and the attacking player loses the RAM they paid.

questions.explanation: As part of declaring attackers, the player runs the attacking characters. A character that is already running cannot be run again. Detain resolves, but the character is already in the state Detain would put it in, so nothing changes. Note this is not a fizzle. The target is still legal. To stop the attack with Detain, use it before the Declare Attackers step.

questions.title: Stamina and the attack cost
questions.situation: Player A declares a character with Stamina as an attacker. Player B responds with an effect that would run that character.
questions.question: What does Stamina change about declaring the attack?

options.text: The character is not run when it attacks, but must still be refreshed to be declared.
The character may attack while already running.
The character cannot be blocked.
The character refreshes immediately after combat damage.

questions.explanation: Stamina is a passive ability that prevents a character from being run as part of the normal requirements for declaring an attack. It does not let a running character attack. The character must still be refreshed to be declared as an attacker. Because a Stamina attacker stays refreshed, Player B's run effect will actually do something here, unlike against a normal attacker.

questions.title: Blockers and blocked attackers
questions.situation: Player A attacks with three characters. Player B wants to assign one blocker to two different attackers, and separately wants to gang-block a large attacker with three characters.
questions.question: Which of these is legal?

options.text: Both are legal.
Neither is legal.
Only the single blocker on two attackers is legal.
Only the gang-block is legal; each blocker may block only one attacker.

questions.explanation: Each blocking character may block only one attacker, but each attacking character may be blocked by multiple blockers. When an attacker is blocked by several characters, the attacking player chooses how to divide its combat damage among them.

questions.title: Legal constructed deck
questions.situation: A player presents a 48-card cyberdeck, a 25-card RAM deck, one mainframe, and a 12-card sideboard.
questions.question: Is this deck legal for constructed play?

options.text: Yes. 48 is above the 40-card minimum.
No. A constructed cyberdeck must contain at least 50 cards.
No. The RAM deck must contain at least 25, not exactly 25.
No. The sideboard is limited to 10 cards.

questions.explanation: A constructed cyberdeck must contain at least 50 cards and no more than 255. The RAM deck is exactly 25 cards. A sideboard may contain up to 12 cards plus one optional mainframe in a dedicated sideboard slot. Everything else in this list is legal. Only the cyberdeck size fails.

questions.title: The four-card limit
questions.situation: A player has three copies of a card in their cyberdeck and wants to add two more copies to their sideboard.
questions.question: Is this legal?

options.text: No. The four-copy limit counts cyberdeck, sideboard, and RAM deck combined.
Yes. The limit applies to the cyberdeck only.
Yes. Sideboard cards are exempt from copy limits.
No. The limit is three copies, not four.

questions.explanation: Except for Basic RAM, no player may include more than four copies of any card with the same name across their cyberdeck, sideboard, and RAM deck combined. Three plus two is five, which is illegal.

questions.title: Mulligans
questions.situation: Player A draws their opening hand of five and dislikes it. They bottom three cards and draw three. They still dislike it and want to mulligan again.
questions.question: May they?

options.text: Yes, but they must bottom one additional card each time.
Yes, as many times as they like.
Yes, up to a maximum of three times.
No. A mulligan may only be taken once.

questions.explanation: Each player draws a starting hand of five and may mulligan once. To mulligan, they place any number of cards from hand on the bottom of the cyberdeck in any order, then draw that many. After resolving, they must keep the hand. The starting player mulligans first, then the others in turn order.

questions.title: Drawing from an empty cyberdeck
questions.situation: Player A's cyberdeck is empty. During their Draw/Install step they choose to draw.
questions.question: What happens?

options.text: Player A loses the game immediately.
The draw simply fails to occur; Player A does not lose.
Player A must install RAM instead.
Player A's recycle bin is shuffled to form a new cyberdeck.

questions.explanation: A player who attempts to draw from an empty cyberdeck does not lose the game. The draw just fails. Neuroscape has no decking loss condition. Note the exception: if a cost requires drawing a card and the cyberdeck is empty, that cost cannot be paid.

questions.title: Does the cache provide synergy?
questions.situation: Player A controls one Cybernetic character in the arena. They play a second Cybernetic character and, while it is still on the cache, try to play a card that requires 2 Cybernetic synergy.
questions.question: Can they play it?

options.text: Yes. The card is on the cache and counts as played.
Yes, but only if the second character is also the same subtype.
No. Synergy comes from persistents in play; the cache is not an in-play zone.
No, and the second character is countered for the illegal attempt.

questions.explanation: Synergy is generated by persistents a player currently controls. A persistent is a card or token in play, and the in-play zones are the arena, the RAM bank, and the environment zone. The cache is not among them. Note also that mainframes are not persistents and generate no synergy at all.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by Pitta on Discord: cards do not provide synergy until they land in the arena.

questions.title: Where does destroyed RAM go?
questions.situation: An effect destroys a RAM card in Player A's RAM bank. A second effect destroys a RAM card that is currently committed to one of Player A's characters.
questions.question: Where do those two RAM cards end up?

options.text: Both return to the bottom of the owner's RAM deck.
The banked one is binned; the committed one returns to the RAM bank running.
Both are purged, since RAM cannot be recovered.
Both go to the owner's recycle bin.

questions.explanation: RAM cards are persistents. When a persistent is destroyed it is binned, meaning it goes to its owner's recycle bin. And that is true whether it was sitting in the bank or committed to a character. Do not confuse this with a character leaving play, which uncommits its RAM back to the bank. Destruction removes the RAM card from the game state entirely. Note that some cards can retrieve RAM from the recycle bin, which is exactly why the destination matters.

questions.title: What can be force quit?
questions.situation: During their Force Quit step, Player A wants to destroy a piece of gear, a RAM card in their bank, and an environment they control.
questions.question: Which of these may they force quit?

options.text: Only the gear. Force quit applies to attachments only.
All three. Any persistent the player controls may be force quit.
Only the gear and the environment; RAM cannot be force quit.
Only characters and programs may be force quit.

questions.explanation: The active player may force quit any number of persistents they control, and persistents include characters, protocols, gear, RAM, and environments. Force quitting RAM is legal and occasionally useful. All persistents force quit during the step are destroyed at the same time, the step does not use the cache, and a player may only attempt to force quit each persistent once per step.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by Sargasso on Discord (August 2026): any persistent can be force quit, including RAM.

questions.title: What counts toward a mainframe requirement
questions.situation: Player A's mainframe ability requires four persistents in play under their control. Player A controls two characters, one gear, and five RAM cards in their RAM bank.
questions.question: Is the mainframe ability operational?

options.text: Yes. Eight persistents are in play, well over the requirement.
Yes, but only if the RAM is refreshed.
No. Only three non-RAM persistents are in play.
No. Gear does not count, leaving only two.

questions.explanation: The hexagon on a mainframe's ability cost bar counts non-RAM persistents in play under the owner's control. Player A has two characters and one gear, which is three. The five RAM cards do not count. The ability is not operational. Mainframes are not persistents themselves and generate no synergy, so the mainframe never counts toward its own requirement either.
questions.changed: CR v1.1 inserted the word 'non-RAM' into 208.6, 208.6a and 303.9a. Under v1.0 the requirement counted all persistents, which meant a full RAM bank could switch on a mainframe ability by itself. That no longer works, and it is a real deckbuilding change rather than a wording cleanup.

questions.title: Revealing face-down cards at the end of a game
questions.situation: Player A wins the game. Player B controls a face-down trojan attached to a mainframe and has two face-down cards in their purge zone.
questions.question: What must happen?

options.text: Player B reveals all face-down cards they own in purge and in play.
Nothing. Hidden information stays hidden once the game ends.
Only the trojan is revealed, since purged cards are out of the game.
Both players reveal their hands as well.

questions.explanation: When a player loses or wins the game, they must reveal all face-down cards they own in purge or in play to all other players. That covers the face-down trojan and both purged cards. Hands are not included. In tournament play this matters: it is how an opponent verifies that a face-down card was what its controller claimed, and a judge should enforce it rather than treat it as optional courtesy.
questions.changed: New in CR v1.1. Version 1.0 had no rule requiring end-of-game reveals.

questions.title: Can you respond to a trigger?
questions.situation: Player A's mainframe deals 2 mainframe damage when they play a Hacker script. Player B is at 1 mainframe health and controls a protocol that gains them health when they play a tarot. Player A plays a Hacker swift script. Player B wants to play a tarot in response to gain health before the mainframe damage lands.
questions.question: Can Player B save themselves?

options.text: Yes. Triggered abilities use the cache, so Player B gets a swift check to respond.
No. Triggered abilities do not use the cache and cannot be responded to at all.
No. The trigger goes on the cache and resolves before the next player gains priority.
Yes. The game does not end until the cache is fully empty.

questions.explanation: Triggered abilities do use the cache, but they resolve before the next player gains priority. When one or more triggers are added, the cache begins resolving until the first non-trigger action is reached. Player B never receives priority in between. The mainframe damage resolves, Player B hits 0 or less mainframe health, and loses as a state-based action.
questions.changed: Rulebook v10.2 stated that triggered abilities do not use the cache and cannot be responded to. Under CR v1.0 they DO use the cache. The outcome here is unchanged, but the mechanism is entirely different, and that difference matters for interactions like Serial Killer's cache manipulation and any effect that counters abilities.

questions.title: Countering an ability
questions.situation: Player A activates a character's ability. Player B holds a swift script that reads 'counter target card.'
questions.question: Can Player B counter the activated ability?

options.text: No. Abilities on the cache are not cards; only effects that specifically counter abilities can target them.
Yes. Anything on the cache is a card for this purpose.
Yes, but the ability's controller may pay 1 RAM to prevent it.
No. Nothing on the cache can be countered once costs are paid.

questions.explanation: Activated and triggered abilities on the cache are not cards. An effect that counters only cards cannot touch them. They may be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Passive abilities can never be countered because they do not use the cache at all.

questions.title: Countered cards and paid costs
questions.situation: Player A plays a character, running four RAM to pay for it. Player B counters it.
questions.question: What happens to the character and the RAM?

options.text: The character returns to hand and the RAM refreshes.
The character goes to the recycle bin and the RAM refreshes.
The character is purged and the RAM returns to the RAM deck.
The character goes to the recycle bin and the RAM stays run. Costs are not refunded.

questions.explanation: To counter a card is to remove it from the cache without resolving it. Countered cards go to their owner's recycle bin and costs paid into them are not refunded. Contrast this with an action reversed for illegality before it reaches the cache, where RAM run to pay costs does become refreshed.

questions.title: Naming is not targeting
questions.situation: Player A plays Genocide, which names a faction and destroys all characters of that faction. Player B wants to respond with The Chariot, which changes the target or targets of a target program.
questions.question: Can The Chariot redirect Genocide?

options.text: Yes. Genocide affects characters, so those characters are its targets.
No. Genocide does not use the word 'target,' so it has no targets to change.
Yes, but only the faction name may be changed, not the affected characters.
No. Tarot scripts cannot target other scripts.

questions.explanation: Cards and abilities can affect objects they do not target. Unless the text specifically uses the word 'target,' nothing is targeted. Naming a faction is a choice made on resolution, not a target declared on the cache. The Chariot has no legal target here, so it cannot be played at all.

questions.title: Redirect does not move the cost
questions.situation: Player A plays Beatdown. Destroy target character, you lose health equal to its attack. Targeting Player B's character. Player B responds with The Chariot and redirects Beatdown onto one of Player A's own characters.
questions.question: Who takes the health loss?

options.text: Player A, because 'you' refers to the card's controller.
Player B, because they redirected it.
Neither. Redirecting cancels the secondary effect.
Both players lose the health.

questions.explanation: Changing a target does not change who controls the card. 'You' and 'your' always refer to the object's controller, which for a played card is the player who played it. Player A loses their own character and takes the health loss. Note also that 'you' never indicates a target.

questions.title: A target becomes illegal
questions.situation: Player A plays gear targeting their own character. Before it resolves, Player B activates an ability that takes control of that character until turn end.
questions.question: What happens to the gear?

options.text: It attaches anyway; control changes do not affect legality.
It attaches to Player B's character and Player B controls the gear.
It returns to Player A's hand.
The target is now illegal, so the gear fails to attach and is binned.

questions.explanation: If a target becomes illegal after being chosen, it is ignored as the effect resolves. CR v1.1 added 113.1d.1, which settles what happens when nothing is left: if all targets have become illegal the effect fails to resolve and is removed from the cache, and a card goes to the recycle bin. The gear had one target, so it is binned. Note the separate state-based action that would also catch this: gear attached to a character with a different controller is binned unless it has the Malicious keyword.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by Bobo and godofacid on Discord.

questions.title: Zero defense
questions.situation: Player A's character has an Armor counter on it, which reads: if this character would be destroyed, remove an Armor counter instead and clear all damage. An opponent's effect reduces the character's defense to 0.
questions.question: Does the Armor counter save it?

options.text: Yes. Reducing defense to 0 destroys it, and the counter replaces destruction.
No. A character with 0 or less defense is binned, not destroyed, so the counter does not apply.
Yes, and the character returns to full printed defense.
No. Armor counters only prevent combat damage.

questions.explanation: This is the single most important distinction in the state-based action list. A character with 0 or less defense is binned. Binning is not destruction, and effects that prevent destruction do not prevent binning. The Armor counter replaces destruction only, so it does nothing here.

questions.title: Counter annihilation
questions.situation: A character has three +1/+1 counters and five -1/-1 counters on it.
questions.question: What is the result the next time state-based actions are checked?

options.text: Nothing. The counters coexist and the net modification is -2/-2.
All eight counters cease to exist.
Three of each cease to exist, leaving two -1/-1 counters.
The controller chooses which set to remove.

questions.explanation: If a persistent has both +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters, N of each cease to exist, where N is the smaller quantity. Three of each are removed, leaving two -1/-1 counters. This matters for any ability that counts counters on the character.

questions.title: When are state-based actions checked?
questions.situation: A judge is called to explain when the game 'cleans itself up.'
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a moment when state-based actions are checked?

options.text: Immediately after an action resolves from the cache.
Whenever an action is placed onto the cache.
At the start of each step and phase.
Between turns, after the Reset Phase ends.

questions.explanation: State-based actions are checked whenever a player would receive priority, immediately after an action resolves, whenever an action is placed onto the cache, at the start of each step and phase, and after a turn-based action finishes. They are explicitly not checked between turns. No events occur there and no player receives priority.

questions.title: Overrun against damaged blockers
questions.situation: An 8-attack character with Overrun attacks and is blocked by a 1/2 and a 1/3. The 1/3 already has 2 damage marked on it from earlier in the turn.
questions.question: How much damage can be pushed through to the defending player?

options.text: 3. Total blocker defense is 5.
5. Blockers require 2 and 1 respectively after accounting for marked damage.
0. Overrun only applies when the attacker is unblocked.
8. Overrun ignores blockers entirely.

questions.explanation: Overrun assigns each blocker damage equal to its defense minus any damage already marked on it, then pushes the excess to the defending player. The 1/2 needs 2, the 1/3 needs only 1 more because it already has 2 marked. That is 3 total, leaving 5 to go through.
questions.changed: Rulebook v10.2 did not account for previously marked damage in the Overrun calculation. Any old ruling that used raw printed defense is now incorrect.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by P1NK (Designer) on Discord (August 2026): Overrun sees how much damage is marked on the blockers.

questions.title: Overrun on defense
questions.situation: In a 2v2 game, a blocking character has Overrun granted by attached gear. Its attack exceeds the attacking character's defense.
questions.question: Does the excess damage go through to the attacking player?

options.text: Yes. Excess damage always carries to the opposing player.
Yes, but only in multiplayer formats.
No. Overrun only functions while the character is attacking.
No, but the blocker's controller may redirect it to a teammate.

questions.explanation: Overrun begins 'while this character is attacking.' A blocking character with Overrun gains nothing from it. Any stat modifications from the gear still apply. The keyword simply does not function on defense.

questions.title: Psychosis on a failed check
questions.situation: During a swift check on Player B's turn, Player A gives all of Player B's non-Thrasher characters +10 Psychosis until turn end. Player B activates one of those characters' abilities, paying 2 RAM and running the character as the cost. The Psychosis roll comes up 4.
questions.question: What happens?

options.text: The ability is removed from the cache, costs stay paid, and the character's attack hits Player B.
The ability resolves anyway; Psychosis only affects attacks.
The ability is removed from the cache and the 2 RAM is refunded.
The character is destroyed.

questions.explanation: Psychosis N triggers when a character would attack or become run by an event that is not declaring an attack. On a roll below N, the character deals damage equal to its attack value to its controller as combat damage, and the action does not occur. If the action was a cost to activate its own ability, that ability is removed from the cache. Regardless of outcome, all costs paid remain paid.
questions.changed: CR v1.1 rewrote 702.11a. Version 1.0 said the character's attack 'instead hits its controller.' It now says the character deals damage equal to its attack value to its controller as combat damage. The practical result is the same, but the new wording is explicit that this is combat damage, which matters for anything keying off combat damage or off an attack hitting.

questions.title: Stacking Psychosis
questions.situation: A character has Psychosis 5 printed, gains Psychosis 10 from an opponent's ability, and gains Psychosis 3 from attached gear. It is declared as an attacker.
questions.question: How many rolls are made and against what number?

options.text: Three separate rolls, against 5, 10, and 3.
One roll against 10, the highest single value.
One roll against 18.
One roll against 5, the printed value.

questions.explanation: N equals the total value of all effects adding Psychosis to the character, and only one instance triggers per event even when multiple instances are applied. The character makes a single roll and fails on a result below 18. Separately, a character with Psychosis 0 or less makes no roll at all and automatically passes.

questions.title: Psychosis from an external run effect
questions.situation: Player A activates an effect that runs Player B's character, which has Psychosis 8. Player B rolls a 3.
questions.question: What happens to Player A's run effect?

options.text: It succeeds and the character is run; the Psychosis attack still hits Player B.
It fails; the character is not run.
It is countered and returned to Player A's hand.
Nothing happens. Psychosis does not trigger on external effects.

questions.explanation: If an external effect causes the character to run, Psychosis still triggers and the roll is still made. But the action that caused it does not fail and occurs as normal. The character's controller still eats the attack damage. This makes external run effects a genuine weapon against high-Psychosis boards.

questions.title: Duel against yourself
questions.situation: Player A activates an ability that duels a target character. Player B flips a trojan that changes the ability's target, redirecting the duel so that Faceless Oni targets itself.
questions.question: How much damage does Faceless Oni take?

options.text: Its attack value twice. Both sides of the duel resolve against it.
None. A character cannot duel itself.
Damage equal to its attack plus its defense.
Its attack value once.

questions.explanation: If a character duels itself, it deals damage equal to its attack value to itself once. Damage dealt during a duel is treated as combat damage.
questions.changed: This reverses the previous community ruling. Under Rulebook v10.2 the accepted answer. Confirmed on Discord by godofacid. Was that a self-dueling character hit itself twice. CR v1.0 explicitly states once. Judges should expect players to argue the old ruling.

questions.title: Trojan timing and card types
questions.situation: Player A plays a trojan face down on Player B's mainframe during their Deploy Phase. Later that same turn, during a swift check, Player A wants to flip and activate it. Player A also controls a mainframe that triggers when they play a Hacker script.
questions.question: Which statement is correct?

options.text: They may activate it this turn, and playing it triggered the script mainframe.
They may not activate it until after the turn it was played; trojans are protocols, not scripts.
They may activate it this turn, but it did not trigger the script mainframe.
They may not activate it until after the turn it was played, but it did trigger the script mainframe.

questions.explanation: Trojan lets its controller flip the card face up and activate its ability during any swift check after the turn it was played, then bin it. Flipping face up and binning are additional costs of activating, and flipping does not use the cache. A face-down trojan keeps its printed card types, subtypes, and tags. It is a protocol, not a script. But has no faction and provides no synergy while face down.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by zerato and Bobo on Discord: all trojans are protocols but not scripts.

questions.title: Choosing the order of replacement effects
questions.situation: A character Player A controls would be destroyed. Two different replacement effects could apply to that destruction event, one from a counter and one from an attached persistent.
questions.question: Who chooses the order in which they apply?

options.text: The affected player, or the controller of the affected object.
The active player.
The player who caused the destruction.
They apply in timestamp order.

questions.explanation: When multiple replacement effects could apply, the affected player or the controller of the affected object chooses the order. Applying one may cause the event to no longer exist, in which case the remaining replacement effects fail to apply. Replacement effects also always apply before prevention effects.

questions.title: Prevented damage and triggers
questions.situation: A character with an ability that triggers when its attack hits a player attacks. All of the damage is prevented by an effect.
questions.question: Does the ability trigger?

options.text: Yes. The attack still connected.
Yes, but the ability's effect is halved.
It depends on whether the prevention effect was a replacement effect.
No. If a damage event is prevented entirely, no triggers requiring damage to be dealt will trigger.

questions.explanation: If a damage event is prevented entirely, no triggered abilities that require damage being dealt will trigger. This applies to Biovamp, Datavamp, Feedback, and any card-specific 'when its attack hits' text.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by P1NK (Designer) on Discord (August 2026), on a Roxy attack into a shard that prevented the damage: an attack hitting requires damage to be dealt.

questions.title: A second copy of an iconic
questions.situation: Player A already controls an iconic character. An effect would create a copy of it under Player A's control.
questions.question: What happens?

options.text: The copy enters play and the original is binned.
The copy is not created.
The copy enters play as a non-iconic token.
The controller chooses which one to keep.

questions.explanation: A player cannot control more than one iconic object with the same name. As a replacement effect, an iconic object being created that shares a name with one you already control is simply not created. If an effect would put such an object into play from another zone, it stays in its previous zone. If an effect would put multiple copies into play at once, choose one and bin the rest.

questions.title: Playing an X card for free
questions.situation: An effect allows Player A to play a card without paying its RAM cost. The card's RAM cost includes X, and the card's text does not define X.
questions.question: What value may Player A choose for X?

options.text: Any number they like. The cost is not being paid anyway.
A number equal to their refreshed RAM.
Only 0.
The card cannot be played this way at all.

questions.explanation: If an effect allows a player to play a card with X in its cost without paying its RAM cost, the only legal choice for X is 0. Note the contrast: effects that merely reduce a cost, even all the way to zero, do not count as 'not paying' that cost, so X may still be chosen freely in that case.

questions.title: One ability between reboots
questions.situation: A character has gear attached that grants it an activated ability. The character activates the gear-granted ability. It also has its own printed activated ability.
questions.question: May it activate the printed ability this turn?

options.text: Yes. Gear abilities and printed abilities are tracked separately.
Yes, if the character is refreshed by another effect first.
Yes, but only during a swift check.
No. A persistent may activate only one of its abilities between reboots.

questions.explanation: A persistent can activate only one of its abilities between reboots. Once it activates any ability, it becomes spent and cannot activate another until it reboots. It stays spent even if it gains or loses abilities in the meantime.

questions.title: Can't beats can
questions.situation: Multiverse allows any number of environments in play. Player A controls Zen Garden, which prevents all damage. Player B plays Mosh Pit, which says damage cannot be prevented.
questions.question: Which effect wins?

options.text: Zen Garden. It was in play first, so it has the earlier timestamp.
Mosh Pit. When one effect permits and another restricts, the restriction wins.
Neither. The two effects cancel and damage is dealt normally.
The active player chooses.

questions.explanation: If one rule or effect permits an action and another effect restricts it, the restriction takes precedence. Can't beats can. Note that timestamp order governs effects within a layer. It does not override a restriction.

questions.title: Damage does not reduce defense
questions.situation: Player A controls a character with 4 defense that already has 2 damage marked on it. Player A wants to play a card whose target requirement is a character with 2 or less defense, and argues the character now qualifies.
questions.question: Is the character a legal target?

options.text: Yes. Marked damage reduces the character's effective defense to 2.
Yes, but only during the combat phase.
No. Damage is marked on the character; its defense is still 4.
No, but it becomes a legal target once the damage is cleared in the Reset Phase.

questions.explanation: Damage dealt to a character causes that much damage to be marked on it. It does not lower the defense value. The character is still a 4-defense character carrying 2 marked damage, and it is not a legal target for a 2-or-less-defense requirement. The state-based action destroys a character when total marked damage equals or exceeds its defense. That comparison is exactly why the two numbers must stay separate. Compare -X/-Y counters, which genuinely do reduce defense.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by P1NK (Designer) on Discord (August 2026): damage does not reduce defence, it increases how much damage is marked on a character.

questions.title: Protocols, trojans, and a full mainframe
questions.situation: Player A is a Mystic player. All three protocol slots on their mainframe are occupied. They hold a protocol whose text box specifies no target, and they want to attach it to Player B's mainframe instead.
questions.question: What happens?

options.text: They may play it targeting only their own mainframe, and on resolution it is binned because no slot is available.
They may attach it to Player B's mainframe, since protocol slots are shared across the table.
They cannot play it at all. The game prevents plays with no legal destination.
They may play it targeting their own mainframe, and one existing protocol is binned to make room.

questions.explanation: When a protocol's text box specifies no target, the only legal targets are the controller's mainframe or a teammate's. Never an opponent's. Trojans are the reverse: trojan text attaches to a target player's mainframe, which is why trojans can be aimed across the table and default protocols cannot. On the slot question, the card is still legal to play. It goes on the cache normally, and only when it resolves with no slot available is it binned. Nothing is displaced to make room.
questions.confirmed: Discussed by Alvin, mania the beekeeper and others on Discord (August 2026). The community answer that a full mainframe means you 'could not play it' is not quite right. You may play it, and it is binned on resolution. Note also that a protocol whose own text specifies a different target may legally target an opponent's mainframe; the restriction is only the default.

questions.title: Redirecting what a protocol does after it lands
questions.cards: The Chariot (Script. Tarot), any protocol with a triggered ability
questions.situation: Player A controls a protocol attached to their mainframe that has a triggered ability. The ability triggers and is placed on the cache. Player B wants to play The Chariot. Change the target or targets of target program. To redirect it.
questions.question: Can The Chariot redirect the triggered ability?

options.text: No, because triggered abilities resolve immediately and never create a swift check.
Yes. The ability originated from a program, so it counts as one.
No, because a triggered ability on the cache is not a program.
Yes, but only if the protocol is still attached when The Chariot resolves.

questions.explanation: The Chariot targets a program. An ability on the cache is not a card and has only the text of the ability that created it. It is not a program, whatever its source was. CR v1.1 added 113.7d.1, which makes this even cleaner: effects that change the targets of a card or ability may only target objects on the cache. The window to redirect a protocol is while the protocol card itself is on the cache, since its target is chosen as it is played. Once it has resolved and attached, anything it generates is a separate object.
questions.changed: Option A is the reasoning currently circulating on Discord, and it was correct under Rulebook v10.2. But it is now false. Triggered abilities DO use the cache under CR v1.0; they simply resolve before the next player gains priority. The conclusion is unchanged, the reasoning is not. Judges should correct the reasoning even when a player reaches the right answer, because the same faulty premise gives the wrong answer for effects that specifically counter abilities.

questions.title: A tether follows the character that leaves
questions.situation: Player A cheats a character into play with an effect that returns it to hand at end of turn, then attaches a tether connecting that character to an established one. At end of turn the cheated character bounces to hand.
questions.question: What happens to the tether and the other tethered character?

options.text: The tether goes to hand with the bounced character; the established character stays in play.
The tether is binned and the established character stays in play unchanged.
Both characters return to hand along with the tether.
The tether reattaches automatically to another eligible character the player controls.

questions.explanation: Tether means that if either character leaves play, the card goes to the same zone as the character that left. The tether follows the bounced character to hand. The established character simply loses the attachment and remains in play. If both tethered characters left simultaneously, the tether's controller would decide which one it follows. Separately, a tether that ends up attached to fewer than two characters is binned.

questions.title: Installing RAM in a modified state
questions.situation: Player A plays a card that installs RAM, and a condition on that card is met such that the RAM enters refreshed rather than in its normal state. Player B wants to respond to the installation.
questions.question: Which statement is correct?

options.text: The modifier is a triggered ability, so Player B may respond to the trigger.
The modifier fails, because installed RAM always enters in the default state.
The modifier applies only if Player A had priority when the RAM entered.
The modifier is a replacement effect; it does not use the cache and Player B cannot respond to the installation itself.

questions.explanation: Effects that change the state a card enters in are replacement effects. They modify how an event occurs rather than triggering off it, and they do not use the cache. Installing RAM likewise does not use the cache and cannot be responded to. Player B's window was in response to the card that caused the installation, not to the installation itself. RAM enters refreshed by default, and effects that say otherwise override the default installation behavior in the same way.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by P1NK (Designer) on Discord (August 2026): it is a replacement effect.

questions.title: Every target becomes illegal
questions.situation: Player A plays a script that targets two characters. In response, Player B removes both of them from play.
questions.question: What happens to the script?

options.text: It resolves with no effect and goes to the recycle bin.
It fails to resolve, is removed from the cache, and goes to the recycle bin.
It stays on the cache until a legal target appears.
It returns to Player A’s hand and the RAM refreshes.

questions.explanation: Individual illegal targets are simply ignored on resolution. But when every target has become illegal, the effect fails to resolve and is removed from the cache. A card removed this way moves to the recycle bin; an ability removed this way ceases to exist. Costs are not refunded either way. The distinction between resolving with no effect and failing to resolve matters for anything that triggers on a card resolving.
questions.changed: New in CR v1.1. Version 1.0 stated only that illegal targets are ignored (113.1d) and never said what happens when nothing is left. This was a genuine gap that judges had to rule around.

questions.title: When an effect does not name a zone
questions.situation: Player A plays a card reading 'destroy all Hacker characters' with no zone specified. Player B has Hacker characters in the arena, in their recycle bin, and one on the cache.
questions.question: Which are affected?

options.text: Only the ones in the arena.
The ones in the arena and on the cache.
All of them, in every zone.
The ones in the arena and in the recycle bin.

questions.explanation: If an effect refers to an object type, subtype, or qualifier without specifying a zone, it refers only to persistents in play of that type. Only the arena characters are affected. There are three exceptions: when the type referred to cannot exist in play at all, such as a mainframe or a script; when the effect replaces or modifies a cost; and when the effect uses game terminology that cannot refer to something in play, such as 'counter' or 'play'.
questions.changed: New in CR v1.1. Version 1.0 had no default-zone rule, which made the scope of any unqualified 'all X' effect a judgment call.

questions.title: A gear ability that names the gear
questions.situation: A piece of gear grants its attached character an activated ability whose text refers to the gear by name, for example 'bin this gear to draw a card.' Player A controls two copies of that gear attached to two different characters.
questions.question: Which gear does the ability refer to when one character activates it?

options.text: Either copy, chosen by the controller.
Both copies, since they share a name.
Neither. The reference is invalid because the ability’s source is the character.
The specific gear the ability came from.

questions.explanation: Normally a name reference in an ability refers to every object with that name, but gear-granted abilities are carved out. An activated ability granted to a character by attached gear keeps a reference to the specific gear it came from, even though the ability's source is now the character. Only that gear is affected. Remember also that activating a gear-granted ability spends the character, so it cannot activate another ability until it reboots.
questions.changed: New in CR v1.1. Version 1.0 had no exception to the name-reference rule for gear-granted abilities, which made 'bin this gear' style text genuinely ambiguous with multiple copies in play.

questions.title: Set versus modify base values
questions.situation: A 2/2 character is affected by three continuous effects, applied in this timestamp order: first, 'this character's base attack and defense are 4/4'; second, 'double this character's base attack'; third, 'this character gets +1/+1.'
questions.question: What are the character's final attack and defense?
questions.explanation: Layer 8 handles attack and defense and has six sublayers applied in order. Layer 8a sets base values, overwriting the printed 2/2 with 4/4. Layer 8b modifies base values, doubling the base attack to 8. Layer 8d applies non-base modifications, adding +1/+1 for a final 9/5. Timestamp order only governs effects within the same sublayer. It never lets a later effect jump an earlier sublayer.
questions.changed: This was Layer 7 in CR v1.0. Version 1.1 inserted a new Layer 6 for ability-adding and ability-removing effects, pushing attack and defense down to Layer 8. The sublayer letters and the logic are unchanged; only the layer number moved.

questions.title: Which layer handles RAM cost?
questions.situation: Two effects apply to a character in play: one sets its RAM cost to 0, and one increases the RAM cost of non-Corpo cards by 1. The character is non-Corpo. The cost-setting effect has the later timestamp.
questions.question: What is the character's effective RAM cost?

options.text: 0. The later timestamp wins.
The controller chooses.
1. Set effects apply in layer 7a, then modify effects apply in layer 7b.
0. Cost-setting effects always override cost-modifying effects.

questions.explanation: Layer 7 covers RAM cost, gear port level, and attack type, and it splits into two sublayers: 7a applies effects that set attributes, 7b applies effects that modify them. The set-to-0 applies first regardless of timestamp, then the +1 modification applies on top, for an effective cost of 1. As a state-based action, one RAM will auto-commit to the character.
questions.changed: This was Layer 6 in CR v1.0. Version 1.1 renumbered it to Layer 7 to make room for the new ability-adding and ability-removing layer.

questions.title: Timestamps and gained abilities
questions.situation: A judge is asked to determine which of two conflicting continuous effects in the same layer applies first.
questions.question: Which of the following does NOT update or create a timestamp?

options.text: An object entering a zone.
An object gaining or losing an ability.
A token being created in the arena.
A mainframe gaining or losing faction synergy.

questions.explanation: Objects entering a zone gain a timestamp, and an object's timestamp updates when it gains or loses an ability. Mainframes are the explicit exception: they always have their ability and only whether it is operational changes, so gaining or losing faction synergy does not affect a mainframe's timestamp.

questions.title: Simultaneous destruction and triggers
questions.situation: Two characters destroy each other in combat. Both have abilities that trigger when their attacks hit.
questions.question: Do both abilities trigger?

options.text: No. Neither character exists when the trigger condition is evaluated.
Yes. The game looks back at the state immediately before they left play.
Only the attacking character's ability triggers.
Only if the controller had priority at the moment of destruction.

questions.explanation: Triggered abilities check the game state immediately after the triggering event and may use information from immediately before it. When multiple objects leave play simultaneously, triggers may look back to determine what existed, which abilities were present, who controlled each object, what caused the event, and how much faction synergy each player had.

questions.title: Synergy at the moment of a board wipe
questions.situation: Player A controls four Mystic persistents. An ability that requires 3 Mystic synergy to remain operational is on one of them. A board wipe destroys all four simultaneously, and one of those persistents has a leave-play trigger gated behind that synergy requirement.
questions.question: Does the trigger fire?

options.text: No. Synergy is recalculated immediately and drops to 0.
Only if the mainframe shares the Mystic faction.
Yes. Persistents leaving play as part of the same event still count toward synergy during that event.
Only if the trigger is placed on the cache before the wipe resolves.

questions.explanation: When an effect, trigger, or rule needs a player's faction synergy at the moment persistents leave play, the game looks back at the state immediately before they left. Persistents leaving as part of the same event still count toward synergy for determining whether abilities trigger, resolve, or remain operational during that event. Synergy is recalculated only once the event finishes and state-based actions are complete.

questions.title: Source of damage after the source is gone
questions.situation: A character with Datavamp deals mainframe damage to a player, then is destroyed before the Datavamp trigger resolves.
questions.question: Does the controller still gain the health?

options.text: Yes. Damage retains its original source, type, and controller even after the source leaves play.
No. The source no longer exists to be credited.
Yes, but the amount is set to 1 because the source's attack can no longer be read.
The opponent chooses whether the trigger resolves.

questions.explanation: Damage retains its original source, damage type, and controller even if that source is no longer in play when the damage occurs or triggers abilities. The game looks back to the source's last known information. This same principle governs which player is credited for a destruction when assigning source of destruction under the state-based action rules.

questions.title: Leaving play and returning
questions.situation: A character reads: 'On enter, until this leaves play, target iconic character you control gets +4/+4. When this leaves play, destroy that character.' It enters, buffs a target, is bounced to hand, and is then replayed, targeting a different character.
questions.question: When the replayed copy later leaves play, which character does it destroy?

options.text: Both. It remembers every character it has ever targeted.
Only the first character, because that link was established first.
Only the second character. Returning to play makes it a new object with no memory.
Neither. The link is broken by the zone change.

questions.explanation: If an object with linked abilities leaves play and returns, it becomes a new object with no memory of previously linked information. The new object's linked abilities cannot access information from its previous existence. The first character keeps nothing and takes nothing; only the second is destroyed. Note the first character also lost the +4/+4 the moment the original left play.

questions.title: Copies and linked information
questions.situation: An effect copies a persistent that has linked abilities and has already tracked a choice made by its first linked ability.
questions.question: What does the copy know?

options.text: Only information created by the copy's own linked abilities after it was created.
Everything the original tracked.
Nothing. Copies never have linked abilities.
The controller of the copy chooses what it remembers.

questions.explanation: A copy tracks only information created by its own linked abilities after the copy was created. It does not inherit previously linked information from the original. Linked abilities also never share information across different objects, even when those objects share a name or copied text.

questions.title: Reversing an action after costs are paid
questions.situation: Player A activates an ability, running three RAM and paying 2 bioframe health as costs. Before the ability is placed on the cache, a judge determines the activation was illegal.
questions.question: What is the correct restoration?

options.text: The RAM stays run and the health stays paid; the action simply fails.
The RAM becomes refreshed but the health is not restored.
The ability is placed on the cache and countered by the rules instead.
The RAM becomes refreshed and the health is restored, which does not count as gaining health.

questions.explanation: If an action becomes illegal after costs are paid but before it is placed onto the cache, costs are refunded if possible and the action is reversed. RAM run to pay costs becomes refreshed, and health costs are restored. Explicitly not treated as gaining health, so nothing that triggers on health gain fires. Once the action has reached the cache, this no longer applies: it is countered by the rules instead, and costs are not refunded.

questions.title: Irreversible actions with hidden information
questions.situation: A player illegally reveals a card from their hand as part of an action that a judge then rules invalid.
questions.question: How does the game restore itself?

options.text: The card is shuffled into the cyberdeck to erase the information.
The card returns to hand if possible; if its location cannot be restored it stays revealed but is treated normally going forward.
The game state cannot be restored, so the game is a draw.
The revealing player must discard the card.

questions.explanation: When a player takes an irreversible and illegal action using hidden information, the game attempts to restore the closest legal state. The card returns to hand if possible. If its location cannot be restored, it remains revealed, but future actions treat it normally. There is no penalty prescribed by the rules themselves. That is tournament policy territory.

questions.title: Retroactive restrictions
questions.situation: Player A legally plays a card. A continuous effect then enters that would have made that play illegal.
questions.question: What happens to the play already made?

options.text: It remains valid; only future actions must follow the new restriction.
It is undone and the card returns to hand.
It is countered by the rules.
The effect that created the restriction is countered instead.

questions.explanation: If a continuous effect makes a once-legal action illegal retroactively, the action remains valid. Only future actions must follow the new restriction. Judges should resist the instinct to rewind here. Nothing was done wrong.

questions.title: What a shortcut may not do
questions.situation: Two players agree to 'go to combat.' The active player intends this to also skip a mandatory state-based action check and a trigger that would otherwise sequence in between.
questions.question: Is this a legal shortcut?

options.text: Yes. Both players agreed, and agreement is the only requirement.
Yes, provided a judge is notified before the round ends.
No, because 'go to combat' is not a recognized shortcut.
No. Shortcuts may not skip mandatory state-based actions or trigger sequencing.

questions.explanation: 'Go to combat' is a recognized shortcut, meaning the active player passes until the Declare Attackers step begins. But a shortcut only changes how players communicate a sequence, never the sequence itself. Shortcuts may not skip mandatory state-based actions, skip trigger sequencing, conceal required decisions, or bypass replacement or prevention effects. Either player may interrupt a shortcut at any legal timing point.

questions.title: Disputed shortcuts
questions.situation: Two players disagree about what game state resulted from a shortcut they took three actions ago.
questions.question: What is the correct resolution?

options.text: The active player's interpretation stands.
Rewind to the last point all players agree on, then proceed without using the shortcut.
The judge chooses the interpretation more favorable to the non-active player.
The game continues from the current state; rewinds are never permitted.

questions.explanation: If players disagree about a shortcut's outcome, rewind to the last point of play that all players agree on, then proceed without using the shortcut. The rules also grant judges authority to define mandatory shortcuts in tournament play to maintain game flow. Worth establishing in your event documentation before disputes arise.

questions.title: Resolving an Unstable mainframe
questions.situation: Player B's mainframe becomes Unstable while they control three characters and two programs. They begin rolling, and the second roll destroys a character that was providing a defensive buff to the others.
questions.question: How does this resolve?

options.text: Roll from lowest RAM cost to highest; each destruction applies immediately before the next roll.
Roll once and apply the result to all persistents.
Roll for all five persistents, announcing each before rolling; everything that fails is destroyed simultaneously afterward.
Roll only for characters; programs are unaffected.

questions.explanation: Unstable means rolling a d20 for each program and character you control, destroying each that rolls 10 or less. The player must announce each persistent before rolling for it. Everything destroyed this way is destroyed at the same time, regardless of the order rolled. So an intermediate destruction cannot change a later roll's outcome. Persistents destroyed this way are destroyed by the rules and have no source of destruction. After all rolls, the mainframe loses Unstable.
questions.changed: Rulebook v10.2 required rolling in order from lowest RAM cost to highest. That sequencing rule is gone, and simultaneous destruction is now explicit.

questions.title: Cost-setting and delayed instability
questions.situation: Player A plays a character that destroys all their RAM and sets the RAM cost of all cards they control to 0 while it remains in play. Several turns later, an opponent destroys it. Player A controls four characters and two programs, with zero RAM in their bank.
questions.question: When does the instability occur and what is rolled?

options.text: Immediately on the cost-setter's destruction; roll for the four characters only.
Immediately on the cost-setter's destruction; roll for all six persistents.
Never. Cost-setting effects are permanent once applied.
At Player A's next System Check step, and the roll covers all six persistents.

questions.explanation: While the cost-setter is in play, layer 7a sets every controlled card's RAM cost to 0, so no RAM is required and there is no shortfall. When it leaves, costs revert and the characters have zero committed RAM. The state-based action tries to auto-commit but the bank is empty, so the shortfall persists. Instability is not immediate: it is checked at the controller's next System Check step, which makes the mainframe Unstable. Unstable then rolls for every program and character controlled. All six. Not just the ones missing RAM.

questions.title: Teammates, control, and synergy
questions.situation: In a 2v2 team match, Player A needs 3 Mystic synergy. Player A controls one Mystic character; their teammate controls four.
questions.question: Can Player A meet the requirement?

options.text: Yes. Teammates share a board for synergy purposes.
No. Synergy counts only persistents that player controls, and teammates do not control each other's cards.
Yes, but only for abilities that reference 'your team.'
Yes, because teammates share health pools.

questions.explanation: A player's synergy equals the synergy generated by persistents they currently control, and characters, gear, and RAM controlled by one player are not controlled by their teammate. Teammates do share health pools and may block attacks against any player on their team, but the boards remain separate. A player may target their teammate only if a card or effect explicitly allows it.

questions.title: Blocking in Free-For-All
questions.situation: In a four-player free-for-all, Player A attacks Player C. Player B has refreshed characters and wants to block to protect Player C.
questions.question: May Player B block?

options.text: Yes. Any player may block any attack.
Yes, if Player C consents.
No. In free-for-all, a player may block only attacks against themself.
Yes, but the blocking characters deal no combat damage.

questions.explanation: In free-for-all, every other player is an opponent and a player may block only attacks against themself. This is the key structural difference from 2v2, where a player may block attacks against any player on their team. Temporary alliances and table talk are permitted but are not binding and have no game effect.

questions.title: Draft pack passing and deck minimums
questions.situation: A judge is setting up a draft pod and is asked to confirm the pack-passing direction and the deck construction floor.
questions.question: Which statement is correct?

options.text: Three packs passed left, right, then left; 30-card cyberdeck minimum; mainframe optional.
Three packs, all passed left; 30-card cyberdeck minimum; mainframe required.
Six packs passed left, right, then left; 40-card cyberdeck minimum; mainframe optional.
Three packs, all passed left; 50-card cyberdeck minimum; mainframe required.

questions.explanation: Draft uses three booster packs per player. The first pack passes left, the second right, and the third left. Cyberdecks must contain at least 30 cards with no maximum. RAM decks are still exactly 25, and Basic RAM need not be drafted. Mainframes are optional; a player without one uses a token mainframe with no abilities. There is no copy limit on drafted cards. Sealed uses six packs and shares the same construction rules.

questions.title: Whose RAM bank refills a stolen character?
questions.situation: Player A controls a character with committed RAM. Player B activates Mind Delver and takes control of it until turn end. On the next swift check, Player A destroys one of the RAM cards committed to that character. The character is now short one RAM.
questions.question: Which player's RAM bank supplies the replacement?

options.text: Player A's, because Player A owns the character.
Neither. The character stays short until control reverts.
Player B's, because Player B currently controls the character.
Player A's, because Player A owns the RAM that was originally committed.

questions.explanation: When a character in play has fewer committed RAM cards than its RAM cost, RAM is attached from its controller's RAM bank as a state-based action, refreshed before running. Control-changing effects apply in layer 2 and do not affect ownership, so Mind Delver's controller is the one who pays. The teaching point is that commitment follows control while ownership governs destination: when the character later leaves play or control reverts, uncommitted RAM returns to its owner's bank, not its controller's.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by P1NK (Designer) on Discord (August 2026) in response to Valentyne's question: the Mind Delver player's RAM.

questions.title: Doubling applies to the final value
questions.situation: Player A attaches gear to a character with 0 Psychosis, and that gear doubles the character's Psychosis. Later in the turn, an opponent's ability adds 10 Psychosis to that character.
questions.question: What is the character's Psychosis value?

options.text: 20. The doubling applies last, to the final total.
0. The doubling locked in at 0 when the gear was attached.
10. The doubling already applied and does not reapply.
The controller of the gear chooses whether to reapply the doubling.

questions.explanation: Psychosis N is the total value of all effects adding Psychosis to the character, and continuous effects are applied continuously rather than locked in at the moment a source enters. The doubling is a modification applied after additions, so it always operates on the current final total. Adding 10 to a doubled 0 yields 20, not 10. The same principle governs base-value doubling in layer 8b, which applies after base values are set but before non-base modifications.
questions.confirmed: Confirmed by P1NK (Designer) on Discord (August 2026): it doubles to 20 because doubling is applied last and will always double the final value. Pitta reached the same conclusion independently.
questions.changed: Note an errata problem that CR v1.1 did not fix. The layer system still assigns no layer to Psychosis value modification. Layer 8 covers attack and defense only, and Psychosis is governed by 702.11a.1 in isolation. Version 1.1 came close: 612.1f.5 now says an ability granted in layer 6 may generate a continuous effect applied in the layer appropriate to the characteristic it modifies, but there is still no layer for Psychosis. The designer ruling is unambiguous, the written rules are not. Cite the designer ruling, not a layer number.

questions.title: Adding and removing abilities in the same layer
questions.situation: A character is affected by two continuous effects. The earlier one grants it Cloaked. The later one causes it to lose all abilities. A judge is asked whether the character has Cloaked.
questions.question: What is the ruling, and would reversing the timestamps change it?

options.text: It has Cloaked either way. Ability-granting is applied in a later sublayer than removal.
It has no abilities either way. Removal always wins over granting.
The controller of the character chooses which effect applies.
No Cloaked now; reversing the timestamps would give it Cloaked.

questions.explanation: Layer 6 handles both adding and removing abilities, and the two are applied together in timestamp order rather than in separate sublayers. Grant-then-remove leaves the character with nothing. Remove-then-grant leaves it with Cloaked. Two related points: an effect that removes all abilities strips both printed abilities and abilities granted earlier in the layer, and removing an ability never undoes effects it has already produced or pulls an ability already on the cache.
questions.changed: Layer 6 is entirely new in CR v1.1. Version 1.0 had no layer for ability-adding and ability-removing effects at all, so this interaction had no written answer.

questions.title: Continuous effects and entering play
questions.situation: Player A controls a passive effect giving all their characters +0/+2. They play a 2/1 character. Player B controls a persistent that triggers whenever a character with 3 or more defense enters play.
questions.question: Does Player B’s ability trigger?

options.text: No. The character enters as a 2/1 and is only boosted afterward.
Yes. Continuous effects apply as the character enters, before triggers are determined.
No. Passive effects do not apply until state-based actions are next checked.
Yes, but only because the boost comes from a passive rather than a counter.

questions.explanation: Continuous effects that modify the characteristics of persistents apply as those persistents enter play, and there is no point at which a persistent is in play without them. These effects are applied before determining whether the persistent entering play causes any abilities to trigger. The character is a 2/3 the entire time it is in play, so Player B's ability triggers. Do not confuse this with a character that enters with counters, which is a replacement effect.
questions.changed: New in CR v1.1. Version 1.0 never stated when continuous effects begin applying relative to entering play, which left the 'does it trigger' question genuinely open.
